hero.tagline: Computer Science student at Webster University. I train small language models from scratch and study when they generalize and when they only memorize. Applying for a thesis-based MSc for Fall 2027.

about.heading: About
about.pull_quote: A software engineer turning to research: I build models, then try to break my own results.
about.bio_1: I am a final-year student at Webster University in Tashkent, completing a B.S. in Computer Science and a B.A. in Economics (May 2027). I come to research from software engineering: I started with C++ and C# desktop applications, taught web development at IT-Academy for two and a half years, and have built production web platforms as a part-time and contract engineer.
about.bio_2: My research question grew out of my own project, MathGen. I trained a 34M-parameter transformer from scratch, and its ~80% accuracy turned out to be mostly memorization: 48.8% of validation samples were copies of training samples. I now run a pre-registered study of when small models generalize and when they memorize, and I am applying for a thesis-based MSc in Computing Science for Fall 2027.

research.heading: Research
research.title: MathGen
research.subtitle: Memorization vs. generalization in a transformer trained from scratch
research.summary: I built a 34M-parameter decoder-only transformer, a hand-written BPE tokenizer and an independent answer verifier, and trained the model from random initialization on synthetic mathematics from 23 problem generators, on a 4 GB laptop GPU. It scored about 80%. Then I audited my own pipeline.
research.finding_leak: 48.8% of validation samples were exact copies of training samples, so the ~80% accuracy measured memorization, not generalization.
research.finding_verifier: The verifier was 100% correct in distribution but wrong on some off-distribution inputs, exactly where generalization is tested. The claimed tokenizer gain was within noise (p = 0.53).
research.finding_study: I rebuilt the evaluation as a pre-registered study with ~5M-parameter models: hash-based splits, held-out value blocks, out-of-range operands and paired seeds.
research.note: Descriptive pilot only. The 36-run confirmatory study has not run yet; null results will be reported as null.
research.oss_megatron: Fixed infinite recursion in the abstract tokenizer's special-token-ID properties, in NVIDIA's framework for training large transformer models.
research.oss_ss166: Added a detection for reflective exec calls through getattr() literals to a security scanner for AI-agent skills.
research.oss_ss167: Added a detection for hidden instructions encoded in Unicode Tag-block characters ("ASCII smuggling").

academic.heading: Academic Profile
academic.objective: A thesis-based MSc in Computing Science starting Fall 2027, followed by a PhD. I want to understand when small language models compute an answer and when they recall one, and to build evaluations that can tell the two apart: deduplicated splits, held-out value ranges and out-of-distribution tests, with multiple seeds and confidence intervals.
academic.ri_memorization_note: When small language models compute answers and when they recall training data
academic.ri_evaluation_note: Deduplicated, held-out and out-of-distribution tests for mathematical reasoning
academic.ri_tokenization_note: How splitting numbers into tokens shapes arithmetic in small Transformers
academic.ri_efficient_note: Training language models from scratch on a single 4 GB GPU
